followUps:
Path validation. The server does not trust the new source address; it sends a PATH_CHALLENGE with random data to that address, and only a client that really receives it can echo the data in PATH_RESPONSE. Until then the server limits what it sends to the new address (anti-amplification, about 3x what it has received).

An attacker who spoofs packets from the victim's address never sees the challenge, so cannot answer, and the victim's address is never used for bulk traffic. Packets are also authenticated, so the attacker cannot forge a valid migrating packet without the keys.

It is reset, because the new path may have completely different capacity and delay. The sender starts again from a small initial window and re-measures round-trip time, instead of assuming the Wi-Fi numbers apply to LTE.

Example: a 200-packet window on Wi-Fi sent into a slow LTE link would cause heavy loss, so QUIC restarts near 10 packets and grows with slow start. If the old path is still usable (a probe on it succeeds), the sender may keep its old estimates for it. Cost: a short throughput dip after the switch, far cheaper than a new handshake.

code.title: Head-of-line blocking: one ordered stream vs per-stream order
code.python:
# Head-of-line blocking: one ordered stream (TCP) vs per-stream order (QUIC)
# Each packet: (sequence number, stream id, arrival time). Packet 1 was lost
# and its retransmission arrives at time 6; the others arrive at time = seq.
packets = [(0, "A", 0), (1, "B", 6), (2, "C", 2), (3, "A", 3), (4, "B", 4), (5, "C", 5)]

# TCP: data is released to the app in sequence order, so a packet waits
# for every earlier packet.
tcp = {}
latest = 0
for seq, stream, arrival in sorted(packets):
    latest = max(latest, arrival)
    tcp[seq] = latest

# QUIC: order is kept only inside each stream.
quic = {}
last = {}
for seq, stream, arrival in sorted(packets):
    last[stream] = max(last.get(stream, 0), arrival)
    quic[seq] = last[stream]

print("packet stream arrival tcp_delivered quic_delivered")
for seq, stream, arrival in packets:
    print(seq, stream, arrival, tcp[seq], quic[seq])
print("TCP total wait:", sum(tcp[s] - a for s, _, a in packets))
print("QUIC total wait:", sum(quic[s] - a for s, _, a in packets))

followUps:
Not much. On a clean network with no loss there is nothing to block behind, so HTTP/3 performs about the same as HTTP/2 over TCP. Its gains appear with loss, high delay or changing networks.

Small wins remain even then: connection setup takes 1 RTT instead of 2 or 3 (TCP plus TLS), and 0-RTT can make resumed requests faster still. The cost is more CPU, since QUIC runs in user space with per-packet encryption, and some networks throttle UDP. On a fast wired link HTTP/2 can even win slightly.

Packet numbers in QUIC are never reused, and Initial, Handshake and Application data each have their own number space. A retransmission gets a new number, so an ACK is never ambiguous about whether it covers the original or the copy.

TCP has the retransmission ambiguity problem: an ACK for sequence 1000 could be for the first send or the resend, which spoils RTT samples. In QUIC every ACK maps to exactly one send time, so RTT and loss estimates are accurate, and handshake loss is detected without being confused by application data.

By storing used tickets (or their binder values) in a store all servers can reach, and rejecting any ticket seen before. A shared fast store such as a replicated cache works; a ticket is accepted only if an atomic insert succeeds.

Alternatives: make tickets single-use by giving each server its own key and routing resumption to the issuer; or use a time window, where the client sends its ticket age and the server accepts it only within, say, 10 seconds and keeps a replay set just for that window. The window keeps the store small. Trade-off: cross-region latency, so many deployments only allow 0-RTT per local cluster.

Not always. The protocol-level GET is meant to be safe, but the server code behind it may have side effects: it may log, count, charge for an API call, send an email or trigger a job.

Example: GET /vote?id=7 that increments a counter would be counted twice if an attacker replays the first flight. Replays can also be used to probe timing (cache hit or miss). So only allow 0-RTT on endpoints you have checked are truly idempotent and cheap, and add a limit on how often early data is accepted.

code.title: BGP best-path selection step by step
code.python:
# BGP best-path selection: compare attributes in order, stop when one decides.
routes = [
    {"name": "provider", "local_pref": 100, "as_path": [10, 20], "origin": 0, "ebgp": True, "igp": 5, "rid": 3},
    {"name": "customer", "local_pref": 300, "as_path": [30, 40, 50, 60], "origin": 0, "ebgp": True, "igp": 9, "rid": 2},
    {"name": "peer", "local_pref": 200, "as_path": [70], "origin": 0, "ebgp": True, "igp": 1, "rid": 1},
]
# Each step: (label, function giving the value where LOWER is better)
steps = [
    ("highest LOCAL_PREF", lambda r: -r["local_pref"]),
    ("shortest AS_PATH", lambda r: len(r["as_path"])),
    ("lowest ORIGIN", lambda r: r["origin"]),
    ("prefer eBGP", lambda r: 0 if r["ebgp"] else 1),
    ("lowest IGP metric", lambda r: r["igp"]),
    ("lowest router ID", lambda r: r["rid"]),
]
candidates = routes
for label, key in steps:
    best = min(key(r) for r in candidates)
    candidates = [r for r in candidates if key(r) == best]
    print(label, "->", [r["name"] for r in candidates])
    if len(candidates) == 1:
        break
print("Best route:", candidates[0]["name"], "(longest AS_PATH, but LOCAL_PREF came first)")

followUps:
To make a path look less attractive to other networks, so they send you less traffic through that link. Each prepend adds your own AS number again, making the AS_PATH longer.

Example: you have two providers, A (main) and B (backup). Announce your prefix to B as 64500 64500 64500 (path length 3) and to A as 64500 (length 1). Remote routers comparing equal LOCAL_PREF pick the shorter path via A, and B only carries traffic if A fails. It is a hint, not a guarantee: routers that rank by LOCAL_PREF first ignore path length.

They are two ways to leave your network. Hot-potato sends traffic out through the nearest exit (lowest IGP cost) to get rid of it quickly; cold-potato carries it inside your network as far as possible and hands it over close to the destination.

Hot-potato is cheaper for you but gives the other network a longer trip and may be asymmetric. Cold-potato gives better latency and control, but costs you backbone capacity. Example: a content network in Tokyo serving a user in Paris hands traffic off in Paris (cold) or in Tokyo (hot). Cold-potato is usually set with MED or communities.

Because maxLength decides how specific an announcement can be and still be valid. If a ROA for 10.0.0.0/16 allows maxLength 24, an attacker can announce a fake 10.0.1.0/24 with your AS number at the end of the path and it still validates as valid, and being more specific, it wins.

With maxLength 16, any /24 is invalid and dropped. Example: a /16 has 256 possible /24s, all of which become safe targets with a loose maxLength. Only loosen it when you really announce those more specific routes.

A hijack is when an AS originates a prefix it does not own. A leak is when a real route is passed on against its business relationship, even though the origin is correct.

Example of a leak: a customer learns routes from provider A and re-announces them to provider B, so B sends traffic through the small customer. The origin is still valid, so RPKI origin validation does not catch it. Leaks are mitigated by prefix filters, max-prefix limits, peer-lock, only-to-customer (OTC) attributes and ASPA. Both cause outages, but the fixes differ.

You withdraw the anycast announcement from that PoP gradually, so users move away before it stops serving. First stop accepting new work (health check fails, or add AS-path prepends to lower its attraction), then wait for existing connections to finish, then withdraw the route.

Steps: prepend 3 times, wait 5 to 10 minutes while traffic shifts, confirm load on the PoP is near zero, withdraw, then do the maintenance. Doing it in this order avoids resetting thousands of connections at once and avoids overloading the next PoP.

Find out why BGP prefers Singapore, then change the announcements, not the user. Check the user's ISP path with a traceroute or looking-glass: usually the ISP has no peering with you near Pune, or prefers a cheaper transit that reaches Singapore.

Fixes: announce the prefix at an exchange or from a PoP in Mumbai or Chennai, peer directly with that ISP, use BGP communities to ask upstreams to prefer a route, or withhold announcement of the prefix from Singapore for that region. As a fallback, use DNS or HTTP redirects based on measured latency.

HTTP/2 puts many requests on one long-lived TCP connection, so a balancer that picks a backend per connection sends all of them to the same server. Load becomes uneven: one client with 100 streams can keep one backend busy while another is idle.

An L7 balancer fixes this by terminating HTTP/2 and choosing a backend per request (or per stream), using its own pool of connections to backends. An L4 balancer cannot see streams at all. Cost: the proxy must manage many concurrent streams and flow control per connection.

You usually cannot do it without looking at more than IP and port, so L4 stickiness is based on a hash of the client address. Hash the source IP (and maybe port) to choose the backend, so the same client always lands on the same server while the backend list is unchanged.

Weaknesses: many users behind one NAT address all land on one backend, and changing the backend list moves clients unless you use consistent hashing. Real stickiness by cookie or session ID needs L7. Typical L4 answer: source-IP hash plus a connection table with a timeout of, say, 30 minutes.

code.title: Hash mod N vs rendezvous hashing when a backend is removed
code.python:
# Hash mod N vs rendezvous hashing when backend 3 is removed (4 -> 3 backends)
M = 4294967296

def h(a, b):
    x = (a * 2654435761 + b * 40503 + 17) % M   # mix flow id a with backend b
    x ^= x >> 15
    x = (x * 40503) % M
    x ^= x >> 13
    return x

def mod_pick(flow, backends):
    return backends[h(flow, 0) % len(backends)]

def rendezvous_pick(flow, backends):
    best = backends[0]
    for b in backends:               # backend with the highest score wins
        if h(flow, b + 1) > h(flow, best + 1):
            best = b
    return best

flows = range(1000)
before, after = [0, 1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 2]
mod_moved = sum(1 for f in flows if mod_pick(f, before) != mod_pick(f, after))
rdv_moved = sum(1 for f in flows if rendezvous_pick(f, before) != rendezvous_pick(f, after))
on_dead = sum(1 for f in flows if rendezvous_pick(f, before) == 3)
print("flows:", len(flows), "backends 4 -> 3")
print("mod N moved:", mod_moved)
print("rendezvous moved:", rdv_moved, "(flows that were on the dead backend:", on_dead, ")")

followUps:
With 100 virtual nodes per backend you usually get about 10 percent load spread, and with around 200 you get closer to 5 percent. Spread falls roughly as 1 over the square root of vnodes.

Reasoning: each backend owns the sum of k random arcs, so its share has relative standard deviation about 1/sqrt(k). With k = 100, that is 10 percent (one standard deviation, so some backends exceed it). For strict plus or minus 10 percent, use about 400 vnodes, or use Maglev or bounded-load hashing, which cap the load directly. More vnodes means a bigger ring to store and rebuild.

Flows go to different backends depending on which balancer they hit, so connections break and the same client may flip between servers. Two balancers with different lists compute different tables, even with identical hash functions.

Example: LB-1 knows backends {A,B,C}, LB-2 knows {A,B,C,D}; a flow mapped to D by LB-2 reaches D, but the next packet via LB-1 goes to C, which has no state and resets it. Fixes: push backend lists as versioned configs from one control plane, add a connection table so established flows stay put, and tolerate short skew with consistent hashing, which limits how many flows differ.

Use IP-in-IP or GRE tunnels (or encapsulation like GUE) instead of rewriting the MAC address. Plain DSR works only in the same layer-2 network because the balancer swaps the destination MAC, which cannot cross a router.

With tunnelling, the balancer wraps the original packet in a new IP header addressed to the backend, which can be anywhere routable. The backend unwraps it and replies directly to the client using the VIP as source. Cost: the extra header (20 bytes for IP-in-IP) reduces MTU, so you must lower MSS or allow fragmentation.

The balancer checks each backend separately, usually by probing the backend's own real address, not the VIP. A TCP connect or HTTP request to the real IP shows whether the service is up.

It cannot rely on seeing responses, because replies skip the balancer. A good check also tests the VIP path inside the backend (the VIP configured on loopback) so a misconfigured backend is not marked healthy. Example: probe every 2 seconds, mark down after 3 failures. Passive health (watching the client's side) is not possible, so active checks are the main signal.

code.title: Stateful firewall with a connection tracking table
code.python:
# Tiny stateful firewall: allow new connections only from inside, track them,
# and let replies back in because they match a table entry.
table = {}        # (src, sport, dst, dport) -> state
MAX_ENTRIES = 2  # finite table, like a real conntrack

def handle(src, sport, dst, dport, inside_src):
    key = (src, sport, dst, dport)
    reverse = (dst, dport, src, sport)
    if key in table or reverse in table:
        return "ACCEPT (established)"
    if not inside_src:
        return "DROP (new connection from outside)"
    if len(table) >= MAX_ENTRIES:
        return "DROP (table full)"   # a flood of new flows can do this
    table[key] = "established"
    return "ACCEPT (new, entry created)"

packets = [
    ("10.0.0.5", 4000, "93.0.0.1", 443, True),   # inside client opens a flow
    ("93.0.0.1", 443, "10.0.0.5", 4000, False),  # the reply
    ("93.0.0.9", 80, "10.0.0.5", 4001, False),   # unsolicited packet
    ("10.0.0.5", 4001, "93.0.0.2", 443, True),   # second flow
    ("10.0.0.5", 4002, "93.0.0.3", 443, True),   # third flow, table is full
]
for p in packets:
    print(p[:4], "->", handle(*p))
print("table size:", len(table))

followUps:
Because an invalid packet does not belong to any known flow or state and should never be allowed by a later, broader rule. Dropping it early also saves work and blocks odd packets used for scanning or evasion.

Example: a stray ACK with no connection, or a packet whose sequence number is far outside the window. If the rule 'accept established' came first it would not match, but an 'accept port 443' rule further down might let the packet in. Putting 'ct state invalid drop' first means the rest of the rules only see packets that are new or part of a real flow. Place 'established,related accept' next, for speed.

NAT stores its address translation inside the conntrack entry. When an inside host (10.0.0.5:4000) connects out, the entry records both the original tuple and the translated one (203.0.113.7:50001).

Reply packets arrive for 203.0.113.7:50001, the table finds the entry and rewrites them back to 10.0.0.5:4000. Every packet of the flow reuses this mapping, so only the first packet needs rule evaluation. It also means NAT and the firewall share the same table, so exhausting it breaks both, and entries must expire (for example 5 days for idle established TCP, seconds for UDP).

A tunnel adds headers, so the packet that fits on the link without a tunnel no longer fits with one. If you ignore this, large packets are fragmented or dropped and connections stall, usually showing up as 'small requests work, big downloads hang'.

Example: Ethernet MTU 1500. WireGuard over IPv4 adds 60 bytes, so the inner MTU is 1420; IPsec ESP adds more, about 50 to 73 bytes. Fixes: set the tunnel interface MTU lower, clamp TCP MSS to match (for example to 1380), and make sure ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages are not blocked.

It means that if a long-term key is stolen later, old recorded traffic still cannot be decrypted. Each session uses fresh temporary keys that are deleted after use.

How: both sides do an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange (for example Curve25519) and derive session keys from it, using the long-term key only to prove identity. An attacker who records traffic today and steals the server key in a year gets nothing. WireGuard rekeys about every 2 minutes, and IKEv2 can use PFS on child SAs. Without it, one leaked key exposes years of traffic.

Look at who is arriving and what they do, not only how many. A flash crowd looks like real users: many different networks and countries, normal browsers, varied URLs, and clicks that follow the usual path (page, then images, then checkout).

An attack tends to look uniform: one or few URLs, the same headers or TLS fingerprint, requests with no cookies or no asset loading, odd source clusters, or a sudden jump with no marketing event to explain it. Also check with the business. When unsure, apply gentle measures such as rate limits, queueing and cached pages, not outright blocking.

Residential botnets use real home IP addresses, which are shared with innocent people and change often. Blocking one IP may block a household of legitimate customers, and the attacker simply rotates to thousands of other addresses.

Example: a blocklist of 10,000 addresses is useless against a botnet of 500,000 that each send only 2 requests per second, which looks normal per IP. Better signals are behaviour, TLS and HTTP fingerprints, challenges, and per-session or per-account rate limits. Blocklists still help against known abusive datacentre ranges.

Because before the client's address is checked, the address could be spoofed, and a big reply would hit the victim. Limiting the server to 3 times the bytes it received means a spoofed packet can gain the attacker at most a 3x amplification.

Example: a 1200-byte client Initial lets the server send up to 3600 bytes before validation. Compare DNS, where a 60-byte request can produce 3000 bytes (50x). Once the client proves it received a server packet (by echoing a token or completing the handshake), the limit is lifted. A Retry packet can force validation first when under attack.

It proves that the sender can receive packets at the address it claims. The server replies with SYN-ACK to the source address, and only the real owner can send back the correct ACK containing the server's sequence number.

A spoofing attacker never sees the SYN-ACK, so it cannot finish the handshake and cannot send data in that connection. This is why TCP services are poor amplifiers: the response to a spoofed SYN is the same size as the request. It does not stop SYN floods, which target the server's state; SYN cookies handle those.
